sutta: Continue with the Nidana Samyutta. We come to Sutta 12.67. On one occasion, the venerable Sariputta and the venerable Mahakassapa were dwelling at Varanasi in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then in the evening, the venerable Mahakassapa emerged from seclusion and approached the venerable Sariputta. They exchanged greetings with the venerable Sariputta. And when And when they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side and said to him, "How is it, friend How is it, friend Sariputta, is aging and death created by oneself, or is it created by another, or is it created both by oneself and by another, or has it arisen or has it arisen fortuitously, being created neither by oneself nor by another?" "Friend Gotama, aging and death is not created by oneself, nor is it created by another, nor is it created both by oneself and another, nor has it arisen fortuitously, being created either neither by oneself nor another, but rather with birth as condition, aging and death comes to be. This fortuitously is the by chance. How is it How is it, friend Sariputta, is birth created by oneself, is existence, clinging, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name and nama-rupa, mentality and materiality, are created by oneself, or is it created by another, or is it created both by oneself and by another, or has it arisen fortuitously, being created neither by oneself nor by another? Mentality and materiality, friend Gotama, is not created by oneself, nor is it created by another, or is created both by oneself and by another, or has it arisen fortuitously? Fortuitously being created neither by oneself nor by another, but rather with consciousness as condition, mentality and materiality comes to be. How is it, friend Sariputta, is consciousness created by oneself, or is it created by another, or is it created both by oneself and by another, or has it arisen fortuitously being created neither by oneself nor by another? Consciousness, friend Gotama, is neither created by oneself nor is it created by another, nor is it created both by oneself and by another, nor has it arisen fortuitously being created neither by oneself nor by another, but rather with mentality and materiality as condition, consciousness comes to be. Now we understand the Venerable Sariputta's statement thus: Mentality and materiality, friend Gotama, is not created by oneself, but rather with consciousness as condition, mentality and materiality comes to be. Now we also understand the Venerable Sariputta's other statement thus: Consciousness, friend Gotama, is not created by oneself, etc., but rather with mentality and materiality as condition, consciousness comes to be. But how, friend Sariputta, should the meaning of this statement be seen? Well then, friend, I will make up a simile for you, for some intelligent people here understand the meaning of the statement by means of a simile. Just as two sheaves of reeds must stand leaning against each other, so too, with mentality and materiality as condition, consciousness comes to be. With consciousness as condition, mentality and materiality comes to be. With mentality and materiality as condition, the six sense bases come to be. With the six sense bases as condition, contact, etc. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. Reverend Sariputta continued, "If friend, one were to remove one of those sheaves of reeds, the other would fall. And if one were to remove the other sheaf, the first would fall. So too with the cessation of mentality and materiality comes cessation of consciousness. With the cessation of consciousness comes cessation of mentality and materiality. With the cessation of mentality and materiality comes cessation of the six sense bases. With the cessation of the six six sense bases, cessation of contact, etc. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering." Let's stop here for a moment. So here, Reverend Sariputta is trying to explain that mentality and materiality and consciousness, they are a pair. They arise together and cease together. Now they stand supporting each other. So when one of them falls, the other also falls. They cannot one cannot exist without the other. So that's why he says in one place he says, "Consciousness conditions mentality and materiality." And on the other hand, he also says that "Mentality and materiality conditions consciousness." So you can say it in either way. Although the Patichchasamuppada, the formula of dependent origination, I say that consciousness conditions mentality and materiality. But as said here, you can also say that mentality and materiality conditions consciousness. Venerable Anuruddha said, "It is wonderful, friend Sariputta. It is amazing, friend Sariputta. How well this has been stated by the Venerable Sariputta. Rejoice in the Venerable Sariputta's statement on these 36 grounds. If friend among teaches the Dhamma for the purpose of revulsion towards aging and death, towards fading away and cessation, he can be called a monk who is a speaker on the Dhamma. If a monk is practicing for the purpose of revulsion towards aging and death, towards fading away and cessation, he can be called a monk who is practicing in accordance with the Dhamma. If through revulsion towards aging and death, towards fading away and cessation, a monk is liberated by non-clinging, he can be called a monk who has attained Nibanna in this very life. Similarly, if if friend among teaches the Dhamma for the purpose of revulsion towards birth or existence of clinging, craving, feeling, contacts, six sense bases, mentality and materiality, consciousness, volition, ignorance, towards fading away and cessation, he can be called a monk who is a speaker on the Dhamma. If a monk is practicing for the purpose of revulsion towards ignorance, towards fading away and cessation, he can be called a monk who is practicing in accordance with the Dhamma. If through revulsion towards ignorance, towards fading away and cessation, a monk is liberated by non-clinging, he can be called a monk who has attained Nibanna in this very life. It's the end of the sutta. So, in this second part, the venerable Sariputta says that uh venerable uh venerable Mahakottitha said that the venerable Sariputta's statement uh he rejoices on 36 grounds. What is this 36 grounds? Uh 36 reasons uh according to the comment to the commentary uh obtained by taking three cases in relation to each of the 12 terms. The first is the quality of being a speaker on the Dhamma. The second is the practice of the Dhamma. The third is the fruit of the practice of the Dhamma. So, three times uh 12 because there are 12 links. So, you get 36. Now, here you see how it says uh if a monk teaches the Dhamma for the purpose of revulsion towards aging and death or for the purpose of revulsion towards any one of these 12 links, uh then he is uh really called a speaker of the Dhamma. So, the purpose of speaking the Dhamma is to teach people to have revulsion towards these uh conditions that give rise to suffering for letting go of the worldly pleasures, uh letting go of the round of rebirth, and then if a monk is practicing for the purpose of revulsion towards uh suffering uh or any of the conditions giving rise to suffering, uh then he is called a monk who is practicing practicing in accordance with the Dhamma. Mhm. And if a person has already achieved revulsion towards suffering and all that, then he's liberated. So, here a real speaker of the Dhamma is one who teaches people to have revulsion towards suffering and all the conditions for suffering. And nowadays, sometimes uh you get people who speak on the Dhamma and they speak on a lot about worldly Dhamma. It's nothing to do with uh the Buddha's teachings. So, that is not called a speaker of the Dhamma.
